facts.statement: The genus of this animal is Echinodon.
facts.quote: genus: Echinodon

facts.statement: The only known species is Echinodon becklesii.
facts.quote: species: becklesii

facts.statement: Sir Richard Owen described the genus in 1861.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Owen, 1861

facts.statement: Sir Richard Owen described the species Echinodon becklesii in 1861.
facts.quote: authority: Owen, 1861

facts.statement: Echinodon lived during the earliest Cretaceous, specifically the Berriasian epoch, in southern England and possibly western France.
facts.quote: lived during the earliest Cretaceous of southern England and possibly western France in the Berriasian epoch

facts.statement: The first specimens discovered were jaw bones named Echinodon becklesii by Sir Richard Owen in 1861.
facts.quote: The first specimens were jaw bones named Echinodon becklesii by Sir Richard Owen in 1861

facts.statement: The specific name becklesii honors the collector Samuel Beckles, who discovered the fossil material.
facts.quote: The specific name honours collector Samuel Beckles who discovered the material of Echinodon

facts.statement: The genus name Echinodon translates to "prickly tooth," referencing its dental anatomy.
facts.quote: the genus name translates as "prickly tooth" in reference to the dental anatomy of the taxon

facts.statement: All known specimens of Echinodon have been found in the Purbeck Group of Dorset.
facts.quote: All specimens of Echinodon have been found in the Purbeck Group of Dorset

facts.statement: Current studies accept an Early Cretaceous Berriasian age for Echinodon, making it the youngest and smallest known heterodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Current studies accept an Early Cretaceous Berriasian age, making Echinodon both the youngest and the smallest heterodontosaurid

facts.statement: Sediments indicate the Purbeck Group was a lagoonal environment similar to the modern Mediterranean that became wetter over time.
facts.quote: the sediments show that the Purbeck Group was a variably lagoonal environment initially similar to the modern Mediterranean but became wetter over time

facts.statement: Multiple jaw bone specimens were discovered by Samuel Beckles on a cliff at Durdlestone Bay on the Isle of Purbeck in southern England.
facts.quote: Multiple specimens of jaw bones were discovered by Samuel Beckles high on a cliff in Durdlestone Bay on the Isle of Purbeck in southern England

facts.statement: Sir Richard Owen named the fossils Echinodon becklesii.
facts.quote: Owen gave the name Echinodon becklesii for the fossils

facts.statement: Owen considered the name Sauraechinodon suggested by Hugh Falconer but chose the unpreoccupied abbreviated form Echinodon.
facts.quote: Owen had corresponded with British palaeontologist Hugh Falconer, who had suggested the name "Sauraechinodon", but as the shortened form Echinodon was not preoccupied, Owen chose to use the abbreviated form as the name for his new animal

facts.statement: Hugh Falconer corrected his proposed name to Sauraechmodon in 1861.
facts.quote: Falconer issued a correction in 1861, specifying that he proposed the name "Sauraechmodon" instead of "Sauraechinodon"

facts.statement: The type specimens designated by Owen were purchased by the British Museum of Natural History in 1876.
facts.quote: The series of specimens designated as types by Owen were purchased by the British Museum of Natural History (BMNH now NHMUK) in 1876

facts.statement: Peter Galton narrowed the depositional locality to the freshwater "Dirt Bed" or "Mammal Pit" excavated by Beckles in 1857 in 1978.
facts.quote: British palaeontologist Peter Galton narrowed down the depositional locality of Echinodon further in 1978 to the freshwater "Dirt Bed", also known as the "Mammal Pit" that was excavated by Beckles in 1857

facts.statement: Peter Galton referred specimen NHMUK 48229, a fragmentary dentary with teeth, to Echinodon.
facts.quote: Galton also referred the specimen NHMUK 48229 to Echinodon, a fragmentary dentary with teeth

facts.statement: The only further referrals to the genus include isolated teeth from the Purbeck beds.
facts.quote: the only further referrals to the genus includes isolated teeth also from the Purbeck beds

facts.statement: Echinodon was originally considered a herbivorous lizard but was quickly revised to be an intermediate ornithischian.
facts.quote: Originally, Echinodon was considered to be a type of herbivorous lizard, though this was quickly revised to an intermediate ornithischian

facts.statement: Echinodon was once referred to the clade Stegosauria based on dental anatomy and incorrectly attributed armor that was later identified as belonging to a turtle.
facts.quote: It was referred to the clade Stegosauria based on general dental anatomy and incorrectly referred armour that was later identified as a turtle's

facts.statement: The age of the Purbeck Group containing Echinodon has been variably considered to be from the latest Jurassic or the earliest Cretaceous.
facts.quote: All specimens of Echinodon have been found in the Purbeck Group of Dorset, which has been variably considered to be from the latest Jurassic or the earliest Cretaceous

facts.statement: There is currently no evidence linking Echinodon to any specific bed in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Group.
facts.quote: However, no evidence exists to link Echinodon to any specific bed in the Lulworth Formation of the Purbeck Group

facts.statement: In 2006, researchers reconsidered material previously assigned to Echinodon and noticed differences in tooth anatomy from the proper species.
facts.quote: In 2006 he reconsidered the material and noticed differences in tooth anatomy from Echinodon proper

facts.statement: The skull of Echinodon was estimated to be 62 mm long based on comparisons with the related genus Heterodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Based on proportions of the related genus Heterodontosaurus, the skull of Echinodon would have been 62 mm long

facts.statement: The premaxilla of Echinodon bore only three teeth that lacked denticles, a feature distinguishing it from most basal ornithischians.
facts.quote: The premaxilla bore only three teeth, lacking denticles (serrations) present in most basal ornithischians

facts.statement: The presence of an arched diastema in Echinodon is a topic of disagreement among paleontologists.
facts.quote: The presence of an arched diastema in Echinodon is a topic of disagreement

facts.statement: Galton and Paul Sereno interpreted a diastema as present in Echinodon, whereas David B. Norman and Paul M. Barrett concluded in 2002 that it was absent based on pre-damage images of the fossil.
facts.quote: While Galton and American palaeontologist Paul Sereno interpret a diastema as present as in Heterodontosaurus, British palaeontologists David B. Norman and Paul M. Barrett concluded in 2002 that, based on the images of Owen prior to later damage of the fossil NHMUK 48209, a diastema was absent

facts.statement: Norman and Barrett suggested the presence of a second caniniform tooth in Echinodon, while Galton (1978) and Sereno (2012) identified only one.
facts.quote: While Norman and Barrett used this as evidence for a second caniniform smaller than the one behind, Galton in 1978 and Sereno in 2012 identified only one canine present

facts.statement: The dentary of Echinodon contained 11 teeth, with the first two being specialized compared to most ornithischians.
facts.quote: There were 11 teeth in the dentary, the first two of which were specialised compared to most ornithischians

facts.statement: Galton (1978) did not discuss specialized anterior teeth in Echinodon, Norman and Barrett (2002) considered them absent, but Sereno (2012) described the first two tooth sockets as differing in size from the others.
facts.quote: While specialised anterior teeth were not discussed by Galton in 1978, and were considered absent by Norman and Barrett in 2002, Sereno described the first two alveoli of Echinodon as differing in size from following teeth in 2012

facts.statement: The dentary of Echinodon was deep for a basal ornithischian, with a height at mid-length of 30% of the total length.
facts.quote: The dentary was deep for a basal ornithischian, its height at mid-length being 30% of the total length

facts.statement: In 1959, Justin Delair referred isolated dermal armour from the Purbeck Beds to Echinodon, but these fossils were later reassigned to solemydid turtles.
facts.quote: Isolated dermal armour found in the Purbeck Beds was referred to Echinodon on the basis of a stegosaurian classification by Justin Delair in 1959, although these have since been reassigned to solemydid turtles.

facts.statement: In 1971, Richard Thulborn placed Echinodon within the family Hypsilophodontidae.
facts.quote: Classifications of many basal ornithischians were reviewed by Richard Thulborn in 1971, where he placed Echinodon within Hypsilophodontidae

facts.statement: Galton considered Echinodon a fabrosaurid because its teeth lacked flat wear facets, despite similarities to Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: However, Galton considered a fabrosaurid identity more likely as the teeth of the taxon lack flat wear facets.

facts.statement: Sereno was the first to reclassify Echinodon as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Sereno was the first to reclassify Echinodon as a member of the family Heterodontosauridae.

facts.statement: In 2011, Pol et al. resolved Echinodon as a basal ornithischian but outside the family Heterodontosauridae, attributing this to the incomplete nature of its remains.
facts.quote: Following additional analysis by South American palaeontologist Diego Pol and colleagues in 2011, Echinodon was resolved as a basal ornithischian, yet not within the family Heterodontosauridae.

facts.statement: According to Sereno (2012), the primary function of Echinodon's premaxillary tooth row was cropping vegetation, indicated by wear patterns and jaw movement.
facts.quote: Based on the presence of wear along the tips of the premaxillary crown and the movement of the dentary caniniform relative to other teeth as the jaw closed, according to Sereno in 2012, the primary function of the premaxillary tooth row would be for cropping vegetation.

facts.statement: Butler et al. (2008) hypothesized that the enlarged canines of the clade were for an omnivorous diet, contrasting with Sereno's vegetation-cropping hypothesis.
facts.quote: This contrasts with the earlier hypotheses of Butler et al. in 2008 that the enlarged canines of the clade were for an omnivorous diet.

facts.statement: Norman et al. (2011) supported an omnivorous diet hypothesis based on the lack of wear on canines and premaxillary teeth.
facts.quote: The hypothesis of omnivory was also supported by Norman and colleagues in 2011 under the interpretation that the canines and premaxillary teeth lacked wear from cropping vegetation.

facts.statement: The type specimen was discovered by Samuel Beckles in the Purbeck Beds near Swanage, England.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo fue descubierto por Samuel Beckles en las Camas Purbeck cerca de Swanage, Inglaterra.

facts.statement: Richard Owen originally thought the fossil was a lizard.
facts.quote: Richard Owen, quien creyó que se trataba de una lagartija.

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the species Echinodon becklesii in 1861, believing it to be a new species of lizard.
facts.quote: Owen creía que era una nueva especie de lagarto que nombró en 1861 como la especie Echinodon becklesii.

facts.statement: The generic name means "hedgehog-tooth," referring to the serrated edge of the tooth.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico significa "diente de erizo", una referencia al carácter puntiagudo del borde del diente aserrado.

facts.statement: The species name honors Samuel Beckles.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie honra a Beckles.

facts.statement: Richard Owen accidentally misspelled the species name as Echinodon becclesii in an illustration caption in 1861.
facts.quote: Owen accidentalmente en 1861 el nombre también como Echinodon becclesii en una leyenda de una ilustración.

facts.statement: Richard Owen declared that no animal had previously been named Echinodon, a fact later confirmed, making Sauraechinodon a junior synonym.
facts.quote: Owen declaró que, hasta donde sabía, ningún animal había sido llamado antes Echinodon y cosa que se confirmó más tarde, por lo que Sauraechinodon debe ser sinónimo más moderno objetivo.

facts.statement: Echinodon lived during the early Cretaceous, approximately 145 to 140 million years ago in the Berriasian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 145 y 140 millones de años, en el Berriasiense, en lo que hoy es Europa.

facts.statement: The genus Echinodon has a time range from the Kimmeridgian to the Berriasian, between 152.21 and 137.05 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Berriasian (152.21 to 137.05 million years ago)

facts.statement: Echinodon was a bipedal herbivore about 60 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Fue un herbívoro bípedo, de alrededor de 60 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: Unlike other ornithischians, Echinodon had one or two canine-like teeth in each jaw.
facts.quote: A diferencias de otros ornitisquios, Echinodon tenía uno o dos dientes caniniformes en cada maxilar.

facts.statement: Echinodon belongs to the family Heterodontosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Heterodontosauridae

facts.statement: The genus Echinodon was established by Owen in 1861.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno concluded in 1991 that the species belongs to Heterodontosauridae based on divergent teeth.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Paul Sereno reclassified Echinodon as a heterodontosaurid in 1991, but this assignment is controversial.
facts.quote: El paleontólogo Paul Sereno lo reclasificó, en 1991, como un heterodontosáurido, pero esta adjudicación es polémica.

facts.statement: David B. Norman and Paul M. Barrett redescribed Echinodon in 2002, supporting Sereno's classification using different evidence.
facts.quote: David B. Norman y Paul M. Barrett redescribieron a Echinodon en el 2002, apoyando la postura de P. Sereno, aunque empleando diferentes pruebas.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno reaffirmed his classification of Echinodon in 2012.
facts.quote: En 2012 Sereno ratifica su adscripción.

facts.statement: Echinodon has occasionally been considered a basal thyreophore, mainly due to the erroneous association of osteoderms from a turtle member.
facts.quote: A Echinodon ocasionalmente se lo ha considerado lo un tireofóro basal, principalmente debido a la asociación errónea de osteodermos del miembro de una tortuga.

facts.statement: If the classification is correct, Echinodon would be the last known member of the group.
facts.quote: Si la tarea es correcta, entonces Echinodon del último miembro conocido del grupo.
